sections.skill: Calculate total and annualized returns, compare nominal and real returns, and describe volatility

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Mia invested $1,000, and five years later it is worth $1,610.51 with no additions. Which annual growth rate, compounded, produces this?
questions.intro: Total return is the percent change over the whole period. The annualized (compound) return is the steady yearly rate that would produce the same result: (ending ÷ starting)^(1 ÷ years) − 1.
questions.feedback: 1,000 × 1.10^5 = 1,610.51, so the annualized return is 10% (total return 61.05%).

misconceptions.C: Divides total growth by 5 years (simple average)

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Mia's investment rose from $1,000 to $1,610.51. What is the TOTAL return?

misconceptions.D: Gives the ending value as a percent

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: An investment returned 8% last year while inflation was 3%. What was the approximate REAL return?
questions.intro: The nominal return is the stated return. The real return adjusts for inflation and shows the change in purchasing power: real return ≈ nominal return − inflation (more precisely, (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1).
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Fund X's yearly returns: 6%, 7%, 5%, 6%. Fund Y's: 20%, −10%, 25%, −11%. Both averaged 6%. Which is more volatile?

choices.text: Neither; volatility is the same as average return

questions.intro: Volatility describes how much returns vary from year to year. Investments with the same average return can have very different volatility; more volatility usually means more risk.
questions.feedback: Fund Y's returns swing widely; Fund X's stay close to 6%.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which statement about investment returns is TRUE?

choices.text: Past returns do not guarantee future returns
An average return will be earned every single year
Returns from last year predict this year exactly
Stocks have never lost money in any year

questions.correct_answer: Past returns do not guarantee future returns
questions.feedback: Averages hide year-to-year swings; the future can differ from the past.

misconceptions.B: Treats an average as a yearly guarantee

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.relationship: Return calculations are percent changes and averages.

questions.prompt: Which set of returns is MOST spread out?
questions.intro: The range (largest − smallest) is a simple measure of spread.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Prices rise 3% and your savings earn 1%. Can your savings buy more or less than before?

choices.text: It cannot be known at all

questions.intro: If prices rise faster than your money grows, it buys less.
questions.feedback: Prices grew faster than the money, so it buys less.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: An investment returns +50% one year and −50% the next. The simple average is 0%. Starting from $1,000, what is it worth?
questions.intro: A simple average of yearly returns can overstate actual growth when returns swing. The compound (annualized) return reflects what really happened to your money.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: For the +50% then −50% example, the compound annual return is about −13.4%. Why is it negative though the simple average is 0%?

choices.text: Losses hit a larger balance than the gains started from

questions.correct_answer: Losses hit a larger balance than the gains started from
questions.intro: Percent changes multiply: a 50% loss after a 50% gain applies to a bigger balance.
questions.feedback: The 50% loss came after the gain, on a $1,500 balance.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: An index rose 20% one year, then 0%, then 20%. Starting at $1,000, what is it worth?
questions.intro: Apply each year's growth factor in turn: multiply by (1 + return) for each year.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: $1,000 grows to $1,210 in 2 years. What steady yearly rate (compound annual growth rate) produces that?
questions.intro: The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) is the single steady yearly rate that turns the starting value into the ending value: start × (1 + rate)^years = end.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A fund ad shows only its best 3-year period. What is the problem?

choices.text: Nothing; the best period is most relevant
It may hide periods of poor performance

questions.correct_answer: It may hide periods of poor performance
questions.intro: Advertisements can choose time periods that look best.
questions.feedback: Cherry-picked periods can mislead; look at standardized 1-, 5-, and 10-year returns.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Using the exact formula, what is the real return on an 8% nominal return with 3% inflation (nearest hundredth)?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A savings account pays 2% while inflation is 4%. What is the approximate real return?
questions.intro: Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation. A negative real return means money loses purchasing power.
questions.feedback: 2% − 4% ≈ −2%: the money buys less each year.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: $1,000 grows to $1,050 in a year when prices rise 5%. What happened to its purchasing power?
questions.intro: Real growth, the change in what money can buy, is about the growth rate of the money minus the inflation rate.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Why do long-term investors care about real returns?

choices.text: Goals like retirement depend on what money will buy
Real returns are always higher than nominal returns
Taxes are based on real returns
Inflation affects only cash, not investments

questions.correct_answer: Goals like retirement depend on what money will buy
questions.feedback: Purchasing power, not the number of dollars, determines what goals can be met.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which asset is MOST likely to lose purchasing power over 30 years?

choices.text: Cash kept in a non-interest checking account

questions.correct_answer: Cash kept in a non-interest checking account
questions.intro: Money that earns nothing loses purchasing power whenever prices rise.
questions.feedback: Zero interest plus inflation steadily erodes purchasing power.

misconceptions.B: Has historically outpaced inflation, with risk

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.
